name: Agent Hardening Sprint
one_liner: Fixed-fee sprint that red-teams a small company's coding agents, MCP servers and CI agent runs, then installs an enforced tool policy and audit trail.

buyer.role: CTO / VP Engineering, or the person who owns SOC 2 or ISO 27001 evidence
buyer.company_profile: B2B SaaS company with 15-150 employees, developers using Claude Code, Cursor or Copilot with MCP servers wired to GitHub, cloud and production data; preparing for or maintaining SOC 2 and receiving customer questionnaires asking how AI coding tools are controlled; no in-house AppSec engineer.

user: The CTO and engineering leads who receive the findings report and policy pack; developers who work under the installed policy; the compliance owner who files the audit evidence.

problem.summary: Small companies adopted coding agents and MCP servers faster than they set rules for them. Permissions are per-developer, MCP tools are auto-approved, headless CI runs auto-approve everything, secrets reach tool inputs, and there is no audit trail. Enterprise platforms sell through large annual commits; leading MCP governance vendors offer no self-serve. These companies need someone to find the real exposure and set up controls they can show an auditor.

evidence.claim: Teams adopting MCP in Claude Code get single-developer setup docs but no governance or security guidance for team adoption.
Wildcard subagents inherited all 16 MCP servers including mail-send and file-delete, and every MCP call default-allowed because the validator did not exist.
Passing secrets as raw input to an MCP tool is a security anti-pattern found in a widely used developer platform.
Users want hooks to stop secrets leaving the machine to the LLM provider and to attackers.
A static capability audit of an MCP server found tools with no operation filtering and SQL tools accepting arbitrary DDL/DML.
Leading MCP governance vendors (Runlayer, MintMCP) publish no prices and offer no self-serve, so small teams cannot evaluate or buy.
External audit connectors and fine-grained authorization require Descope Growth at $799/mo; lower tiers keep audit for 1 week to 1 month.
In non-interactive -p runs the Antigravity CLI auto-approves all tool calls including write_file, making it unsafe for automation that processes untrusted input.

why_now.summary: All major coding agents now expose enforceable pre-tool-call hooks or policy engines (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Gemini CLI), so a consultant can install real controls with free building blocks instead of selling a platform. OWASP's Top 10 for Agentic Applications (Dec 2025) gives auditors and buyers a reference list to ask about, and clouds (AWS AgentCore Policy GA, March 2026) are normalising per-tool-call authorization as an expected control.

features.feature: Inventory script (run by the client) that collects each developer's agent configs, permission rules, hooks and MCP server list, plus a workflow scanner that flags CI agent steps triggered by untrusted events with write permissions or secrets; secrets stripped
features.why: Most teams do not know which agents, MCP servers and CI agent jobs are in use; this scopes the engagement in a day.

features.feature: Hands-on prompt-injection red team: planted issues, poisoned files and malicious MCP tool output against the client's real agent setup, documented as reproducible findings
features.why: Turns abstract risk into evidence a CTO acts on; uses the founder's offensive-testing skills.

features.feature: Policy pack: one YAML policy compiled into each agent's native hooks/managed settings by open-source hook scripts that parse commands (shell AST) rather than match strings
features.why: Delivers enforced controls with free building blocks and closes the compound-command bypass of pattern-based native rules.

features.feature: CI agent hardening: read-only default for headless runs, automatic downgrade to read-only when job input is untrusted issue/PR text, and a canary secret that fails the run if it appears in tool input or output
features.why: Headless runs auto-approve tool calls with nobody watching; this targets the main injection path deterministically.

features.feature: Audit logging from hooks into the client's existing log store, plus a control narrative mapped to OWASP agentic risks and SOC 2 change-management evidence
features.why: The compliance owner gets something to file and show customers.

features.feature: Monthly retainer: policy updates as agents change, review of blocked-call logs, re-test after new MCP servers
features.why: Recurring revenue and the data to later productise the most repeated work.

out_of_scope: Building a hosted SaaS platform in year one
Security of the client's own AI product (LLM app pentests) beyond the developer toolchain

competitors.name: Knostic Kirin
competitors.how_we_differ: A self-serve tool for scanning and policy; we deliver a tested setup, red-team findings and audit evidence, and can recommend Kirin where it fits.

competitors.name: Native agent permissions and managed settings
competitors.how_we_differ: Free but someone has to design, test and maintain the rules across agents; that is the service.

competitors.name: Docker MCP Gateway (open source)
competitors.how_we_differ: Free container isolation for MCP servers with no per-user policy or audit without the enterprise version; we can recommend it alongside the hook policy, which also covers shell and file tools.

competitors.name: Pillar Security / Lasso Security
competitors.how_we_differ: Enterprise platforms bought through annual commits; we are a fixed-fee engagement priced for small companies.

competitors.name: Runlayer / MintMCP
competitors.how_we_differ: Enterprise MCP gateways with unpublished, quote-only pricing; we set up controls without a new gateway.

competitors.name: General pentest and vCISO firms
competitors.how_we_differ: Usually test the product, not the developer toolchain; we specialise in coding-agent and MCP exposure with a reusable policy kit.

differentiation: A narrow specialist service with a productised kit: inventory and CI workflow scan, real prompt-injection tests against the client's own agents, and enforced controls installed through native hooks at a fixed price, with audit evidence for a SOC 2 auditor. No platform licence or gateway. The open-source kit, one compiled policy refined across engagements, is the seed of a later product.

build.team: 1 technical founder (solo, bootstrapped); subcontract a second tester only once demand exceeds 2 engagements per month
hardest_parts: Building credibility in AI-agent security quickly, since the founder's track record is Windows detection and CTFs rather than LLM tooling
Making the red-team phase reproducible and safe on clients' real repos and credentials
Keeping the hook-based policy kit and its shell-command parser current across four fast-changing agents and their headless modes, without false positives
Finding buyers without paid ads or an existing client base

pricing.model: Fixed-fee assessment and setup, then optional monthly retainer
pricing.entry_price: $3,500 fixed fee for up to 25 developers (2-week sprint: inventory, red team, policy pack, audit setup); retainer $400/month
pricing.rationale: Well under enterprise annual commits (Lasso $20k+) and comparable to a year of Descope Growth, but one-off and tied to evidence the buyer needs now. Three to four sprints a month plus a handful of retainers reaches a solo founder's income target in months, with near-zero running cost.

comparables.price: AWS Marketplace annual commit $20,000 (GenAI Chatbots), $50,000 (LLM gateway)

go_to_market.first_customers: Ten 15-150 person B2B SaaS companies that use coding agents with MCP servers and are in a SOC 2 cycle or answering enterprise customer questionnaires about AI tooling; reached first through the founder's few industry contacts, then through referrals from SOC 2 readiness consultants and vCISOs who lack agent expertise.
go_to_market.channel: Founder-led: public red-team write-ups and talks at local security meetups and BSides; partnerships with SOC 2 readiness consultants/vCISOs who resell the sprint; LinkedIn outreach to CTOs; and outbound to companies whose public repositories run agents on untrusted issue/PR events, found with the workflow scanner and sent a short exposure note.
go_to_market.wedge: A free 30-minute 'agent exposure check' using the inventory script, ending with a one-page list of the three worst findings and a quote for the sprint.

risks: Services do not scale and depend entirely on the founder's time; productising the kit later may take longer than planned.
Credibility: buyers may prefer established AppSec firms; the founder must build public proof (write-ups, open-source kit) before deals close.
Bundling: as agent vendors ship organisation-wide managed policies and dashboards, the setup work shrinks and the buyer may do it alone.
Demand risk: small companies may treat agent security as a low priority until an incident or an auditor forces it.

Liability: red-teaming clients' real agents with production credentials could cause damage; needs scoped rules of engagement and insurance. CI controls run in the same runner as the agent and are a guardrail, not a sandbox, and must be sold as such.

riskiest_assumption.assumption: CTOs or compliance owners at 15-150 person SaaS companies will pay a few thousand dollars now for coding-agent and MCP hardening, before an incident or explicit auditor requirement.
riskiest_assumption.test: Offer the free agent exposure check to 30 companies via the founder's contacts, two SOC 2 consultants and LinkedIn; run the checks with the inventory script and quote the $3,500 sprint at the end of each.
riskiest_assumption.success_signal: At least 8 checks booked and at least 2 signed sprints (or deposits) within 2 weeks.

open_questions: Do SOC 2 auditors and enterprise questionnaires already ask specific questions about coding agents, or is this still optional?
Which work is repeated across engagements and could become a product (variant v1 or v2)?
Will SOC 2 consultants partner or see this as competition?
How long will it take the founder to build recognised credibility in AI-agent security?
Is unattended CI agent hardening a strong enough pain on its own to lead the sale, or only an add-on to the developer-laptop work?
revision_log: [variant v2] Headless/CI coverage in the policy pack: read-only default for CI agent runs, automatic downgrade when the job input is untrusted issue/PR text, and a planted canary secret that fails the run if it appears in tool input or output

[variant v2] Agent-workflow scanner: reads .github/workflows and flags agent steps triggered by untrusted events with write permissions or secrets; used in the inventory and, on public repos, as an outbound lead source

[variant v1] Hook scripts evaluate commands by parsing them (shell AST) instead of string patterns, and the kit keeps one YAML policy compiled into each agent's native hook/policy format as the path to a later product
